title: April 2025 Class End of Block Exam

sets.title: Set 1: Original Exam Questions
sets.description: The original MCQs from the April 2025 class Block One Exam paper (PHM 102: Pharmacology Paper One, Section A, Q1 to Q30). Q4 has two True/False statements, (a) and (b), each listed as its own question.

questions.text: Mucolytic drugs are indicated in treatment of:
questions.explanation: Chronic bronchitis (C) is correct because mucolytics (acetylcysteine, carbocisteine, bromhexine, ambroxol) break down or thin thick, sticky bronchial secretions so that they can be coughed up more easily. They are therefore used in conditions with thick, difficult-to-clear sputum such as chronic bronchitis and COPD, bronchiectasis and cystic fibrosis. The patient should be encouraged to drink plenty of fluids and to do chest physiotherapy, and be warned that they will cough up more sputum at first. Asthma (A) is treated with bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids; mucolytics can irritate the airways and may trigger bronchospasm. Rhinitis (B) is treated with antihistamines, nasal corticosteroids or decongestants. Pharyngitis (D) is a throat inflammation treated with analgesics, throat lozenges and antibiotics only if bacterial; it does not involve thick bronchial mucus.

questions.text: An example of methylxanthine bronchodilator is:
questions.explanation: Aminophylline (D) is correct because it is a methylxanthine, a combination of theophylline with ethylenediamine that makes it water soluble for IV use. Methylxanthines relax bronchial smooth muscle by inhibiting phosphodiesterase (raising cyclic AMP) and blocking adenosine receptors, and they are used in severe asthma and COPD. They have a narrow therapeutic range (theophylline blood level about 10 to 20 mcg/mL), so the nurse watches for toxicity: nausea and vomiting, tachycardia, palpitations, restlessness, tremor and seizures, and gives IV aminophylline slowly. Smoking, some antibiotics (erythromycin, ciprofloxacin) and cimetidine change blood levels. Acetylcysteine (A) is a mucolytic and is also the antidote for paracetamol overdose. Albuterol, also called salbutamol (B), is a short-acting beta-2 agonist. Atrovent (C), ipratropium bromide, is an anticholinergic bronchodilator.

questions.text: An adverse effect of codeine antitussive is:
questions.explanation: Respiratory depression (C) is correct because codeine is an opioid that suppresses the cough centre in the medulla, and at higher doses or in susceptible patients (children, older people, those with COPD, or with other sedatives or alcohol) it also depresses the respiratory centre. Other effects are drowsiness, constipation, nausea, dizziness, and dependence with long use. It is avoided in children, in breastfeeding mothers and in respiratory failure, and the patient is advised not to drive or drink alcohol. Insomnia (A), tachycardia (B) and arrhythmias (D) are stimulant effects and are typical of sympathomimetic decongestants such as pseudoephedrine, and of methylxanthines, not of opioids, which tend to slow the heart rate and cause sedation.

questions.text: True or False: Chlorpheniramine can cause drowsiness and sedation.
questions.explanation: TRUE. Chlorpheniramine is a first-generation H1 antihistamine. These drugs cross the blood-brain barrier and block histamine and other receptors in the brain, which causes drowsiness and sedation. They also have anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention and constipation. The patient should be warned not to drive or operate machinery, to avoid alcohol and other sedatives, and that the drug is best taken at night. Second-generation antihistamines such as loratadine and cetirizine cause much less sedation.

questions.text: True or False: Dextromethorphan a non-narcotic antitussive.
questions.explanation: TRUE. Dextromethorphan is a non-narcotic cough suppressant that works centrally by raising the threshold of the cough centre in the medulla. It is chemically related to opioids but does not act on the opioid receptors in the way codeine does, so at normal doses it does not cause analgesia, significant respiratory depression or dependence. Side effects are mild: dizziness, drowsiness and nausea. In large doses it can cause hallucinations and abuse, and it should not be given with monoamine oxidase inhibitors or with some antidepressants (SSRIs) because of the risk of serotonin syndrome.

questions.text: Antibiotics that inhibit cell wall formation in bacteria include:
questions.explanation: Amoxicillin, ceftriaxone (A) is correct because amoxicillin (a penicillin) and ceftriaxone (a cephalosporin) are beta-lactam antibiotics. They bind penicillin-binding proteins and block the cross-linking of peptidoglycan in the bacterial cell wall, so the wall is weak and the bacteria burst (bactericidal). Linezolid, chloramphenicol (B) inhibit protein synthesis at the 50S ribosomal subunit. Doxycycline, erythromycin (C) also inhibit protein synthesis (doxycycline at 30S and erythromycin at 50S). Gentamycin, lincomycin (D) are protein synthesis inhibitors too (gentamicin at 30S and lincomycin at 50S). Other cell wall inhibitors are vancomycin, bacitracin, carbapenems and monobactams. Human cells have no cell wall, which is why these drugs are selectively toxic to bacteria.

questions.text: The treatment effect produced when clavulanic acid is combined with amoxicillin in treatment of pneumonia is:
questions.explanation: Synergistic (B) is correct because the combined effect is greater than the effect of amoxicillin alone. Many bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus, H. influenzae and Moraxella produce beta-lactamase enzymes that break the beta-lactam ring of amoxicillin and make it inactive. Clavulanic acid has very little antibacterial action by itself, but it binds and inactivates these enzymes, which protects amoxicillin so that it can kill the bacteria, widening its spectrum (co-amoxiclav). Antagonistic (A) would mean one drug reduces the effect of the other. Additive (C) would mean the effect is just the sum of two drugs that both work against the bacteria, which is not the case here because clavulanic acid alone does not treat the infection. Agonistic (D) is not a term for a drug combination effect; an agonist is a drug that activates a receptor. Common side effects of co-amoxiclav are diarrhoea and, rarely, cholestatic jaundice.

questions.text: The correct prescription of gentamycin for a child with severe pneumonia weighing 10kg and whose plan for gentamycin is 3mg/kg/day for 5 days is:
questions.explanation: IV 15mg BD for 5/7 (A) is correct. The daily dose is 3 mg/kg/day x 10 kg = 30 mg in 24 hours. BD means twice a day, so the 30 mg is divided into two doses of 15 mg every 12 hours, and 5/7 means for 5 days. Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside that is not absorbed from the gut, so it must be given parenterally (IV or IM), which makes the oral options P.O 15mg BD for 5/7 (B) and P.O 30mg BD for 5/7 (C) incorrect. IV 30mg BD for 5/7 (D) is incorrect because it gives 60 mg a day, which is double the plan (6 mg/kg/day) and would risk nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Nursing care: check the dose calculation, give IV doses slowly, and monitor urine output, kidney function and hearing. Note that many paediatric guidelines now give gentamicin once daily at a higher mg/kg dose, but this question gives the plan as 3 mg/kg/day.

questions.text: The aminoglycoside with least nephrotoxic and ototoxic adverse effects is:
questions.explanation: Tobramycin (B) is the best answer because among these four it has the lowest combined risk of kidney and ear toxicity: several comparative studies and the drug label report that tobramycin causes nephrotoxicity less often than gentamicin, and it has less ototoxicity than kanamycin and streptomycin. Gentamycin (A) is more nephrotoxic than tobramycin because it accumulates more in the renal proximal tubule, and it damages both the cochlea and vestibular system. Kanamycin (C) is more strongly ototoxic (especially to hearing) and nephrotoxic. Streptomycin (D) actually has the lowest nephrotoxicity of the group, but it is markedly toxic to the vestibular system (dizziness, vertigo, imbalance), so it does not have the least ototoxicity. Note: because streptomycin is the least nephrotoxic aminoglycoside on its own, this item depends on the phrase 'nephrotoxic and ototoxic' together, which points to tobramycin.

questions.text: Treatment of choice for cystitis is:
questions.explanation: Cefadroxil (D) is the best answer among the options. Uncomplicated cystitis (infection confined to the bladder, mostly E. coli) is treated with an oral antibiotic for a short course: nitrofurantoin is the usual first choice where available, and oral first-generation cephalosporins such as cefadroxil or cephalexin are recommended alternatives (co-trimoxazole is used where local resistance is low). Cefadroxil is well absorbed after oral administration and excreted unchanged in the urine in high concentrations. Levofloxacin (A) is a fluoroquinolone, kept in reserve for when other drugs cannot be used because of adverse effects (tendon rupture, QT prolongation, CNS effects) and resistance. Gentamycin (B) and ceftriaxone (C) are injectable drugs that are reserved for complicated infections such as pyelonephritis and sepsis, and are not needed for a simple bladder infection. Nursing advice: finish the course, drink plenty of fluids, and pass urine regularly.

questions.text: A radical cure for malaria is:
questions.explanation: Primaquine (A) is correct because a radical cure means eliminating all parasite forms from the body, including the dormant liver stages (hypnozoites) of Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale that cause relapses. Primaquine kills these liver forms (usually given for 14 days after a blood schizonticide), and a single low dose also kills P. falciparum gametocytes, which reduces transmission. It can cause haemolysis in G6PD deficiency (test first), abdominal upset and methaemoglobinaemia, and it is avoided in pregnancy and in infants under 6 months. Halofantrine (B), mefloquine (C) and quinine (D) are blood schizonticides that clear the parasites from the red blood cells and treat the acute attack, but they do not kill the liver hypnozoites, so relapses can still occur. Halofantrine is also cardiotoxic (QT prolongation) and is no longer recommended.

questions.text: In management of severe malaria, intravenous quinine should be administered in:
questions.explanation: 5% dextrose (D) is correct because quinine stimulates the pancreas to release insulin and can cause hypoglycaemia, and severe malaria itself also lowers blood glucose, especially in children and pregnant women. IV quinine is therefore diluted in 5% dextrose (10% in some settings) and given as a slow infusion over about 4 hours (never as a rapid bolus, since this causes hypotension and arrhythmias). The nurse monitors blood glucose regularly, the ECG or pulse, blood pressure, and signs of cinchonism (tinnitus, deafness, nausea). Ringers lactate (A), 0.9% saline (B) and 0.45% saline (C) do not supply glucose to protect against hypoglycaemia. Where available, IV artesunate is now preferred to quinine for severe malaria because it reduces mortality, and quinine is used when artesunate is not available.

questions.text: A long-acting anti-malarial drug used as a prophylaxis is:
questions.explanation: Mefloquine (A) is correct because it has a long half-life of about 2 to 3 weeks, which allows it to be taken once weekly for prophylaxis (started 2 to 3 weeks before travel, continued during the stay, and for 4 weeks after leaving the malaria area). It must be avoided in people with epilepsy, depression or other psychiatric illness, and in those who are taking drugs that prolong the QT interval, because it can cause vivid dreams, anxiety, dizziness and psychosis. Primaquine (B) is mainly used for the radical cure of vivax and ovale malaria and has a short half-life. Fansidar (C), sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, is also long-acting, but it is used for intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy and not as the usual long-acting prophylaxis for individuals; it can cause serious skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome). Amodiaquine (D) is used in treatment with artesunate and in seasonal malaria chemoprevention, and has risks of liver toxicity and agranulocytosis. Note: Fansidar is also long-acting, but mefloquine is the classical long-acting prophylactic drug.

questions.text: A patient with chicken pox is treated with:
questions.explanation: Acyclovir (A) is correct because chickenpox is caused by the varicella-zoster virus, which is sensitive to acyclovir. Acyclovir is converted by viral thymidine kinase into acyclovir triphosphate, which blocks viral DNA polymerase and stops viral replication. It works best when given within 24 hours of the start of the rash, and is mainly used in adults, pregnant women, newborns, immunocompromised patients and severe cases (IV in severe disease, with good hydration to prevent crystal nephropathy). Healthy children are mostly treated symptomatically with paracetamol, calamine lotion and trimmed nails, and aspirin must be avoided because of Reye's syndrome. Amantadine (B) is used for influenza A and Parkinson's disease. Foscarnet (C) is used for CMV infections and acyclovir-resistant herpes viruses. Raltegravir (D) is an integrase inhibitor used for HIV.

questions.text: A non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor include:
questions.explanation: Nevirapine (D) is correct because it is a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI). NNRTIs bind directly to a site on the reverse transcriptase enzyme and change its shape so it cannot copy HIV RNA into DNA, and they do not need to be activated in the body. Others in this class are efavirenz, etravirine and rilpivirine. Nevirapine can cause skin rash, which may become severe (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), and hepatotoxicity, so it is started at a lower lead-in dose for 14 days, and liver function and skin are monitored. Dolutegravir (A) is an integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI), which blocks integration of viral DNA into the host genome. Tenofovir (B) and lamivudine (C) are nucleoside (or nucleotide) reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), which are false building blocks that stop DNA chain growth.

questions.text: The antifungal used for treatment of fungal meningitis is
questions.explanation: Fluconazole (A) is correct because it penetrates well into the cerebrospinal fluid and brain tissue, and it is available as oral and IV forms. In cryptococcal meningitis (the commonest fungal meningitis, especially in advanced HIV), the standard treatment is induction with amphotericin B (with flucytosine), followed by high-dose fluconazole for consolidation, then lower-dose fluconazole as maintenance (and sometimes fluconazole alone where amphotericin is not available). Side effects are nausea, headache, rash and hepatotoxicity, and it interacts with many drugs because it inhibits liver enzymes. Clotrimazole (B) is only used topically for skin and mucosal candidiasis. Griseofulvin (C) is used for dermatophyte infections of the skin, hair and nails, and does not reach the CSF. Itraconazole (D) has poor penetration into the CSF, and is used mainly for histoplasmosis, blastomycosis and sporotrichosis.

questions.text: The drug of choice in management of ringworms is:
questions.explanation: Griseofulvin (B) is correct because it is the classic oral drug of choice for ringworm (tinea) infections of the scalp, skin and nails, especially tinea capitis in children. It is fungistatic: it is deposited in new keratin and prevents fungal mitosis, so the infected keratin is replaced by healthy keratin as it grows, which is why long treatment is needed (weeks to months). It is best taken with a fatty meal to improve absorption. Side effects are headache, nausea, photosensitivity (use sun protection) and hepatotoxicity; it is teratogenic and contraindicated in pregnancy (contraception is needed during and after treatment), and it reduces the effect of warfarin and oral contraceptives. Amphotericin B (A) is a toxic IV drug used for severe systemic fungal infections. Ketoconazole (C) is restricted because of hepatotoxicity. Itraconazole (D) is an alternative that is more expensive. Terbinafine is now preferred for tinea in adults in many places, but griseofulvin is still the classic answer.

questions.text: Nitrofurantoin is used in the treatment of:
questions.explanation: Uncomplicated urinary tract infections (C) is correct because nitrofurantoin is excreted in the urine in high concentrations, where it acts as a bactericidal antiseptic against common causes of cystitis such as E. coli, but it reaches very low levels in blood and tissues. It is therefore used only for lower UTI (cystitis) and prophylaxis against recurrent UTI, and not for kidney infection or any infection outside the urinary tract, which makes respiratory tract infections (A), peritonitis (B) and genital ulcers (D) incorrect. It should be taken with food or milk to reduce nausea, it turns the urine dark yellow or brown, and it is avoided in significant renal impairment, G6PD deficiency, and near term in pregnancy and in infants under 1 month. Long-term use can cause peripheral neuropathy and lung and liver reactions.

questions.text: Mechanism of action of aluminium hydroxide is:
questions.explanation: Neutralizing the gastric acid (C) is correct because aluminium hydroxide is a non-systemic antacid, a weak base that reacts with hydrochloric acid in the stomach to form aluminium chloride and water, raising the gastric pH and also reducing the activity of pepsin. It gives quick but short-lasting relief of heartburn and dyspepsia and helps ulcer healing. It is given 1 and 3 hours after meals and at bedtime, and other oral drugs are given 1 to 2 hours apart, since antacids reduce absorption of many drugs. Its main side effect is constipation (often balanced with magnesium hydroxide, which causes diarrhoea), and it binds phosphate and can cause low phosphate in long use, and aluminium can build up in kidney failure. Inhibition of histamine receptors (A) describes the H2 blockers such as ranitidine. Blocking of gastric secretion (B) describes proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole. Increase of mucosal blood flow (D) is related to prostaglandin analogues such as misoprostol.

questions.text: The class of drug that is contraindicated in patients on salicylates is:
questions.explanation: Bismuth compounds (C) is correct because bismuth subsalicylate (as in some anti-diarrhoeal and anti-ulcer products) is broken down in the gut to bismuth and salicylic acid, and so it adds to the salicylate dose and can lead to salicylate toxicity (tinnitus, nausea, confusion, acid-base disturbance) in a patient already on aspirin or other salicylates. It is also avoided in children and teenagers with viral infection because of the risk of Reye's syndrome, and it causes a harmless black tongue and black stools. H2-receptor antagonists (A) and proton pump inhibitors (B) are often given together with aspirin to protect the stomach, and they do not contain salicylate. Antacids (D) are not contraindicated, although they should be separated from aspirin by 1 to 2 hours, and by making the urine alkaline they can increase salicylate excretion.

questions.text: An example of an osmotic cathartic is:
questions.explanation: Polyethylene glycol (C) is correct because it is an osmotic laxative: it is not absorbed from the gut and holds water in the bowel lumen by osmosis, which softens and increases the volume of stool and stimulates peristalsis. Other osmotic laxatives are lactulose and magnesium salts (milk of magnesia, magnesium sulphate) and phosphate enemas. Large volumes of polyethylene glycol are used for bowel cleansing before colonoscopy or surgery, and the patient must be encouraged to drink plenty of fluids; the nurse watches for dehydration and electrolyte imbalance. Psyllium (A) is a bulk-forming laxative, which swells with water and needs plenty of fluid. Bisacodyl (B) is a stimulant laxative that irritates the bowel wall nerves. Docusate sodium (D) is a stool softener (surfactant) that lets water enter the stool.

questions.text: Metoclopramide acts by:
questions.explanation: Inhibition of dopamine receptors (C) is correct because metoclopramide is a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist. In the chemoreceptor trigger zone it blocks dopamine and so prevents nausea and vomiting, and in the gut it blocks the inhibitory effect of dopamine and also stimulates 5-HT4 receptors, which increases gastric emptying and lower oesophageal sphincter tone (a prokinetic). It is used for nausea and vomiting, gastro-oesophageal reflux and delayed gastric emptying. Because it also blocks dopamine in the brain, it can cause drowsiness, restlessness and extrapyramidal effects (dystonia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia), especially in young people and with prolonged use, and it is contraindicated in intestinal obstruction, perforation and bleeding, and in Parkinson's disease. Decreasing gastrointestinal motility (A) is the opposite of its effect. Coating the gastric mucosa (B) describes sucralfate. Blocking muscarinic receptors (D) describes hyoscine and atropine.

questions.text: Aspirin produces antiplatelet effect by inhibiting:
questions.explanation: Cyclooxygenase-1 (C) is correct because aspirin irreversibly acetylates cyclooxygenase-1 in platelets, which stops the production of thromboxane A2, a substance that makes platelets aggregate and blood vessels constrict. Platelets have no nucleus and cannot make new enzyme, so the effect lasts for the life of the platelet (7 to 10 days), even with low doses (75 to 150 mg daily), which is why low-dose aspirin is used to prevent heart attack and stroke. Lipoxygenase (A) makes leukotrienes and is not inhibited by aspirin (zileuton blocks it). Phospholipase A2 (B) is the enzyme inhibited indirectly by corticosteroids. Cyclooxygenase-2 (D) is mainly responsible for the anti-inflammatory and pain effect and is inhibited more weakly by aspirin; the coxibs selectively inhibit it. The main risk of aspirin is gastric irritation and bleeding.

questions.text: A selective COX-2 inhibitor include:
questions.explanation: Celecoxib (C) is correct because it is a coxib, a selective COX-2 inhibitor. COX-2 is produced at sites of inflammation, whereas COX-1 protects the stomach lining and helps platelets to aggregate, so selective COX-2 inhibition gives pain and anti-inflammatory relief with less stomach ulceration and bleeding and no effect on platelets. However, coxibs increase the risk of heart attack and stroke and cause fluid retention and hypertension, so they are avoided in ischaemic heart disease, stroke and heart failure, and they are contraindicated in patients with sulfonamide allergy (celecoxib). Diclofenac (A), ketorolac (B) and piroxicam (D) are non-selective NSAIDs that inhibit both COX-1 and COX-2, and so can cause gastric ulceration and bleeding, and kidney injury; ketorolac in particular has a high risk of GI bleeding and is limited to short courses.

questions.text: Drug of choice in management of malignant hyperthermia is:
questions.explanation: Dantrolene (C) is correct because malignant hyperthermia is a life-threatening hypermetabolic reaction of skeletal muscle triggered by volatile anaesthetic gases (halothane, sevoflurane) and succinylcholine, with a rapidly rising temperature, muscle rigidity, tachycardia, rising end-tidal carbon dioxide, acidosis and hyperkalaemia. Dantrolene blocks the ryanodine receptor and so stops the release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum of muscle, which stops the uncontrolled muscle contraction and heat production. It is given as a rapid IV bolus (2.5 mg/kg, repeated as needed). Other management includes stopping the trigger agents, giving 100% oxygen, hyperventilation, active cooling (cold IV fluids, ice packs), treating hyperkalaemia and arrhythmias, and monitoring urine output. Midazolam (A) and diazepam (B) are benzodiazepines that sedate or treat seizures but do not treat the muscle calcium problem. Neostigmine (D) reverses non-depolarising muscle relaxants and is not a treatment for this condition.

questions.text: The antidote for a benzodiazepine overdose is:
questions.explanation: Flumazenil (C) is correct because it is a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine binding site of the GABA-A receptor, and quickly reverses sedation and respiratory depression from drugs such as diazepam and midazolam. It is given IV in small increments. Its action is short (about 1 hour), shorter than many benzodiazepines, so the patient can become sedated again and must be observed for several hours. It can cause seizures, especially in patients who are dependent on benzodiazepines, in epilepsy, or in mixed overdose with tricyclic antidepressants, so it is used with caution. Airway support and oxygen remain the first priority. Naloxone (A) reverses opioids. Physostigmine (B) is used for anticholinergic poisoning. Atropine (D) treats bradycardia and organophosphate or cholinergic poisoning.

questions.text: Gingival hyperplasia is a side effect of:
questions.explanation: Phenytoin (C) is correct because overgrowth of the gums (gingival hyperplasia) is a well-known adverse effect of long-term phenytoin, more common and marked in children and adolescents and in people with poor oral hygiene. The nurse should teach careful brushing with a soft brush, flossing and regular dental review. Other effects include nystagmus, ataxia, drowsiness, hirsutism, coarse facial features, folate deficiency, osteomalacia, many drug interactions through enzyme induction, and fetal hydantoin syndrome in pregnancy; IV phenytoin must be given slowly with cardiac monitoring. Diazepam (A) causes sedation, respiratory depression and dependence. Carbamazepine (B) causes dizziness, double vision, hyponatraemia, rash (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) and blood disorders. Phenobarbitone (D) causes sedation, hyperactivity in children, and osteomalacia.

questions.text: Neuromuscular blocking agents are primarily used to produce:
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle relaxation (A) is correct because neuromuscular blocking agents (succinylcholine, atracurium, rocuronium, vecuronium, pancuronium) interrupt transmission at the neuromuscular junction by acting on nicotinic receptors at the motor end plate. They cause paralysis of skeletal muscle to allow endotracheal intubation, to give good operating conditions in surgery, and to allow mechanical ventilation in intensive care. They have no sedative, pain-relieving or amnesic effect, so the patient must always be given adequate anaesthesia or sedation and analgesia and be ventilated, because a paralysed patient can still be aware and feel pain. Antispasmodic effects (B) refer to relaxing smooth muscle of the gut (hyoscine). Local anesthesia (C) is the effect of drugs such as lidocaine. Antianxiety effects (D) are those of benzodiazepines.

questions.text: An adverse effect associated with overdose of acetaminophen is:
questions.explanation: Hepatotoxicity (B) is correct because in an overdose the normal metabolic pathways of acetaminophen (paracetamol) become saturated, and more is converted by CYP450 to a toxic metabolite called NAPQI. Normally it is neutralised by glutathione, but in overdose the glutathione stores are used up, and NAPQI damages liver cells, causing centrilobular liver necrosis and acute liver failure (raised liver enzymes and INR, jaundice, hypoglycaemia and encephalopathy). The early stage may have only nausea and vomiting, so any suspected overdose must be treated. The antidote is N-acetylcysteine, which replaces glutathione, and it is most effective if started within 8 to 10 hours; activated charcoal may be given in early presentation. Risk is higher in alcoholics, malnourished patients and those with existing liver disease. Gastrointestinal bleeding (A) is an effect of NSAIDs and aspirin. CNS depression (C) and respiratory depression (D) are effects of opioids and sedatives.

questions.text: First-line management of acute gout attack is:
questions.explanation: Colchicine (C) is correct among the options because it is a first-line drug for an acute gout attack (together with NSAIDs and corticosteroids). It binds tubulin and stops white blood cells (neutrophils) from moving into the joint and releasing inflammatory substances, so it reduces the inflammation caused by uric acid crystals, and works best when started within 12 to 36 hours of the start of the attack. Its main side effects are nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, which are early signs of toxicity, and the dose must be lowered in kidney or liver disease. Allopurinol (A) lowers uric acid production and is not started in an acute attack because it can worsen or prolong it. Morphine (B) is not used for gout, as it does not treat the inflammation. Probenecid (D) increases uric acid excretion and is used for long-term prevention, and starting it during an acute attack can make it worse.

questions.text: Reye's syndrome occurs when Aspirin is given to children with:
questions.explanation: Viral infection (C) is correct because Reye's syndrome is a rare but serious condition that happens when aspirin (salicylates) is given to children and teenagers who have a viral illness, most often influenza or chickenpox (varicella). It causes acute swelling of the brain (encephalopathy) and fatty infiltration and damage of the liver, with persistent vomiting, confusion, seizures, coma and hypoglycaemia. For this reason, aspirin is avoided in children with fever or viral illness, and paracetamol is used instead. Chronic arthritis (A) is a condition where aspirin was used in the past, but Reye's syndrome is not caused by arthritis itself; modern treatments are safer. Bacterial infection (B) is not the trigger. Allergy to penicillin (D) has no connection with Reye's syndrome.
